name: Wire size
seoDesc: Wire size: work out maximum wire temperature from the source voltage and the allowable voltage drop. A free physics calculator with the formula, units and…
summary: Give the Wire size calculator the source voltage, the allowable voltage drop, the current and the one-way distance and it returns maximum wire temperature. Think of it as a shortcut for a lab report, a problem set or a sanity check on a physical situation. The unit chips sit next to the boxes, which is where most hand-calculation mistakes start.

sections.title: How does the Wire size calculator work?
sections.html:
The Wire size calculator takes the values in the form, applies the relationship described below and reports maximum wire temperature in the results panel.

Working from the top of the form: you choose the option that describes your case (the electrical system and the conductor material); then you type in the source voltage, the allowable voltage drop (V), the current (I) and the one-way distance (L).

Press Calculate and the page works through the equation with the values you supplied and derives the rest; it then keeps up with you as you correct a typo.

Because the equation can be rearranged for each of its variables, the page also runs backwards. Leave the box you want to know empty, fill in the rest, and it solves for the missing one instead. That is useful when you know the answer you need rather than the inputs you have.

sections.title: What do you need to enter?
sections.html:
• Pick the option that matches your case — 2 options, such as DC/AC Single-phase and AC Three-phase. The choice changes which relationship the calculator applies, not just a multiplier, so it is worth reading the options carefully.
  • A measured quantity, entered by default in volts. The unit chip switches it to any of the 6 supported units.
  • A measured quantity, entered by default in percent. The unit chip switches it to any of the 6 supported units.
  • Pick the option that matches your case — 2 options, such as copper (1.68 µΩ⋅cm) and aluminum (2.65 µΩ⋅cm). The choice changes which relationship the calculator applies, not just a multiplier, so it is worth reading the options carefully.
  • A measured quantity, entered by default in amperes. The unit chip switches it to any of the 3 supported units.
  • A measured quantity, entered by default in meters. The unit chip switches it to any of the 34 supported units.
  • A measured quantity, entered by default in square millimeters. The unit chip switches it to any of the 24 supported units.

2 fields on this form are a choice rather than a number. Those choices decide which version of the calculation applies, so they are worth setting before you worry about the digits.

sections.title: The formula behind the Wire size calculator
sections.html:
The page rests on a handful of relationships. Each one can be rearranged for any of its variables, which is what makes the calculator work in both directions:

Maximum wire temperature=(1 ÷ 2) × allowable voltage drop (V) × source voltage × wire cross-sectional area (A) ÷ (conductor Resistivity × current (I) × one-way distance (L) × electrical system × temp coefficient) + 20 − 1 ÷ temp coefficient
Wire gauge=(wire cross-sectional area (A))
Wire diameter (d)=2 × the square root of (wire cross-sectional area (A)) ÷ the square root of (PI)
Wire cross-sectional area (A)=(current (I), maximum wire temperature, conductor Resistivity)
Wire gauge=((current (I), maximum wire temperature, conductor Resistivity))
Wire diameter (d)=2 × the square root of ((current (I), maximum wire temperature, conductor Resistivity)) ÷ the square root of (PI)

Read it as an ordinary equation. Where a word appears instead of a letter, it is the label of one of the boxes in the form; where a function appears, it is the usual mathematical meaning of that function.

sections.title: How are units and precision handled?
sections.html:
Every quantity with units carries a chip beside its box. Switching the chip does not change what you know, only how it is written: values are converted to a common internal base, the arithmetic happens there, and the answer is converted back for display. Mixing metres with feet in one calculation is therefore safe.

  • Voltage, opening in volts
  • %, opening in percent
  • Electric current – ampere, opening in amperes
  • Length, opening in meters
  • Temperature, opening in Celsius
  • Area, opening in square millimeters
  • Length, opening in millimeters
  • Area, opening in square millimeters

Display rounding is separate from calculation rounding: the digits you see are shortened, the value behind them is not. Numbers far from everyday size are shown in scientific notation so the significant digits stay readable.

sections.title: When should you use it?
sections.html:
The Wire size calculator earns its place in the middle of a task, not instead of one. It is most useful when:

  • Writing up a lab result and needing a quick cross-check
  • Solving a problem set where the algebra is more interesting than the arithmetic
  • Testing whether an answer is physically plausible before you trust it
  • Any time the same 4 figures keep coming back — the source voltage, the allowable voltage drop and the current — and you would rather not repeat the arithmetic by hand each time.

sections.title: How do you get a reliable answer?
sections.html:
• Round only at the end. The calculator carries full precision internally, so re-entering a value you already rounded is the fastest way to introduce drift.
  • If a result surprises you, look at the order of magnitude before the digits: a plausible number in the wrong unit looks more convincing than an implausible one, and is easier to miss.
  • Compare two scenarios by changing the input that actually differs between them, and keep the rest fixed, so the difference you see is the difference you meant to test.
  • Write the answer down with its unit. A bare number copied into a report later is exactly where units get lost.

sections.title: What else is worth knowing?
sections.html:
• Filling in more than one box is fine. The most recently edited field is the one treated as known, so you can switch direction without reloading.
  • Answers that depend on a drop-down reflect the option you picked, not a range. Switching to a neighbouring option is the quickest way to see how much that factor matters.
  • Some options are backed by reference tables that ship with the page, so the values are fixed data rather than a live lookup.
  • Fields that are still blank are exactly the ones the calculator has not yet been given, so the results panel is a reliable map of what is missing.

faq.q: What does the Wire size calculator work out?
faq.a: It returns maximum wire temperature, derived from the source voltage, the allowable voltage drop and the current. Every field in the form feeds the same relationship: press Calculate once and changing any of them updates the result immediately, with no page reload.

faq.q: What do I need to enter to use the Wire size calculator?
faq.a: The form asks for the source voltage, the allowable voltage drop, the current and the one-way distance, which is 7 fields in total. Each one is labelled with what it means and, where relevant, the unit it expects. Anything you leave blank is treated as the value to solve for.

faq.q: Can I enter source voltage in a different unit?
faq.a: Yes. Source voltage opens in volts and the chip beside it offers 6 units. The number you typed keeps its magnitude and only its label changes; the calculation itself happens in a common base unit, so mixing systems in one form is safe.
Yes. Each variable in the relationship can be the one being solved for: fill in the answer you are aiming at, leave the field you want empty, and the calculator inverts the equation for you.

faq.q: How much do the drop-down choices change the answer?
faq.a: There are several choices to make (2 in total), and each one selects a different case rather than scaling the result. Switching a single option and watching the result is the fastest way to see how much that choice is worth.

faq.q: Is the Wire size calculator free to use?
faq.a: Yes — no account, no sign-up and no limit on how many times you run it. The arithmetic happens in your browser, so the values you type are not sent anywhere.
